power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Searching for variability: The role of listener choice on learning new words
table.research_questions:
In this study, we are testing whether preschool-aged learners choose to hear words produced by multiple talkers, the extent to which they seek out this variability (e.g., as many speakers as possible, from just one speaker, or something in between) and how that relates to their learning. Further, we will then ask whether actively seeking variability, compared to the variability structure being selected for the participant, has an impact on learning. 

Participants in Experiment 1 will be told that they are going to play a game where their job is to learn to say some new words and to learn their meanings, and that they can learn these words from up to 8 different people. Participants will learn names for 6 novel objects. These nouns follow conventional rules of English and are produced by five males and five females, ages 18-24. The objects are selected from the NOUN database. The experiment consists of five parts: introduction, familiarization, learning, production test, and comprehension test. During the introduction, participants will see a cartoon image of a hand centered on the screen, surrounded by 8 different color icons representing different speakers. Each color icon will light up, and participants will be asked to click on it to hear each speaker say, “hi, it’s nice to meet you.” In the familiarization trial, participants will see an apple in the center of the screen with the same 8 icons surrounding it. They will be told they can choose who to hear the word from, 8 different times, in any combination. This trial is repeated with an image of a ball. The introduction and familiarization phases are included so that participants have heard each speaker and know what they sound like, and understand the general task of clicking on an icon and hearing that speaker label the object in the center. Once participants click on a speaker icon, the icons disappear from the screen and only the central image remains while they hear it labeled, before they go back to seeing the icons to choose from.

Then, on each training trial, participants will see one of the 6 images centered on the screen, surrounded by the 8 speaker icons. Trials for each word will be blocked, such that participants hear each word 8 times before moving on to the next item. Participants will be told that they can select who they want to hear it from, and that they can choose to hear the same person multiple times, different people, or some combination of the two. We will record who participants choose to hear the word from. As above, after clicking a speaker icon, the speaker icons disappear so that they only see the target image while hearing it labeled by that speaker. After 48 trials (6 nouns X 8 repetitions), participants will advance to the test phase, which is described in the dependent variables section.

Participants in Experiment 2 will also be told that they are going to play a game where they learn some new words but they will not be given the choice of who to hear them from. Instead, the choices from a yoked participant from Experiment 1 will be used. The speaker introduction phase will be identical to Experiment 1. In the training phase, participants will still see one of the images centered on the screen, surrounded by 8 different colored icons representing different speakers. Instead of having the option to select who they would like to hear the words from, the speaker selected by their yoked participant will light up, and participants will click on it to hear the word. By asking participants to click on the speaker icon we are matching the motor movements of participants across Experiments.
table.design_dependent_variables: Following the learning phase, there are two test phases, which we will use as our two dependent variables:  comprehension accuracy and production accuracy. During the production test, participants will first see an image on the screen and be asked to label it. We will first start with a practice using pictures they already know the labels to (apple, ball), followed by the newly learned words.  Each picture will be presented twice, in random order. Participants’ responses will be recorded for later analysis, using the tablet’s microphone as well as an external recorder. Participants will then complete a comprehension test, during which they will hear a prompt to touch or click on one of the pictures. We will start with practice pictures they are already familiar with (apple, ball). Then, they will see all 6 newly-learned images on the screen at once and will be asked to find each one, once by a novel female speaker and once by a novel male speaker. Comprehension accuracy will be binary coded as correct or incorrect on each trial. Participants’ productions will be transcribed by trained research assistants, compared to target productions, and then binary coded as correct or incorrect, following the protocol laid out by Sinkeviciute et al., (2019). For both comprehension and production, binary accuracy coding allows us to use logistic regression for the analyses, avoiding issues that might arise from non-normality (see Sinkeviciute et al., 2019).
table.study_design_overview: There are two between subjects conditions, which we are treating as separate experiments as Experiment 1 will be conducted in full before Experiment 2, but the data will be compared. The first group of participants will be in the active choice condition, such that they are able to select who they want to hear the words from on each trial. The second group of participants will be in the passive condition, and each participant will be matched to one of the active choice participants and receive a yoked passive exposure.
table.statistical_tests:
For the training data, we will calculate the number of different talkers selected for each word (ranging from 1-8), as well as the Entropy (an information theoretic measure of variability) of the series of selections, referred to as Talker Entropy below. A higher Talker Entropy number would reflect more variability in what talkers were selected (the Talker Entropy calculation for someone who selected each speaker once would be 3), while a lower Talker Entropy number would reflect no variability (the Talker Entropy calculation for someone who selected one speaker eight times would be 0). These measurements will be used to descriptively answer RQ1: do children seek out talker variability during word learning? 

RQ2 asks how the variability learners sought out relates to production and comprehension accuracy, and RQ3 asks whether imposing a specific sampling pattern changes the effects on learning. To answer these question, we will conduct logistic regressions testing whether production accuracy (0/1) or comprehension accuracy (0/1) are predicted by the number of talkers/Talker Entropy, active or passive experience and the interaction between the two, with by-word and by-participant random effects. Within each outcome (production/comprehension) we will test whether the model with number of talkers or talker entropy accounts for more variance through model comparisons. 

The model formulas are as follows: 
ProductionAcc (0/1) ~ NumberTalkers*Experiment (Active/Passive) + (1|Subj) + (1|Word)
ProductionAcc (0/1) ~ TalkerEntropy*Experiment (Active/Passive) + (1|Subj) + (1|Word)
ComprehensionAcc (0/1) ~ NumberTalkers*Experiment (Active/Passive) + (1|Subj) + (1|Word)
ComprehensionAcc (0/1) ~ TalkerEntropy*Experiment (Active/Passive) + (1|Subj) + (1|Word)
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
We will not exclude outliers, as it would be difficult to determine what an outlier is given a relatively small range of possible performance. 

Our pilot data reveals that some participants do not attempt to provide responses during the production phase (e.g., saying they don’t know and don’t want to guess). We will exclude participants from the production test if they did not produce any of the target words during the production test (e.g., they only labeled the words in English, or said they don’t know). Since we expect this to be more common than if we were testing adults, this will not be a criteria for exclusion from the comprehension test analyses.  
We will also exclude participants from these analyses if they are exposed to a language other than English > 25% of the time, though we will collect data from non native English speaking participants and analyze it separately if we recruit a sufficiently large sample size.
table.sample_size:
Each participant will hear each of the 6 words 8 times (48 trials), and be tested on production twice per word (12 trials) and twice on comprehension for each word (12 trials). 
In their research on talker variability and second language learning, Sinkeviciute et al. (2019) had a sample of 32 7- and 8-year-olds, which was deemed sufficient based on Richtsmeier et al. (2009) that had a final sample of 32 4-year-olds. We will test 40 3 and 4 year old participants in Experiment 1 and 40 different 3 and 4 year old participants in Experiment 2, as our task has less well defined conditions (e.g. no 1 talker vs. 8 talkers), increasing variability in the learning and potentially test phases.
table.additional_comments:
In addition to logistic by trial analyses reported above, we will also test whether more vs. less variability across the experiment, calculated as average number of talkers and average talker entropy on a participant level is related to average production and comprehension accuracy. 

If we find that binary coding of the production test items is too coarse of a measure of accuracy, we will instead use the approach taken by Barcroft and Sommers (2005), coding partial errors and allowing for a mistake by 1 phoneme (edit distance of n=1)  to still be considered correct. 

As a last resort, we will then creating average accuracy scores instead. In this case, we would be unable to look at the data on a trial-by-trial basis.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 216 columns across 27 data files.
#### Issues Identified

15 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

summary_table.ethics_statements: This study was approved by the University at Buffalo IRB and we obtained informed consent from participants' parents before data collection.
live_data_statements: Participants were then tested on their learning of the novel words, both in production and comprehension.

If active information seeking is beneficial more generally, or if participants are choosing talker variability that is optimally useful or interesting for them, then we expect a benefit for learning in the Active condition.

Forty participants were assigned to the Active condition, and 40 were assigned to the Passive condition (see below), participant age (t (78)=0.08, p=.938) and sex (t (77) = -0.56, p=.574) did not differ between the Active and Passive condition.
Participants were recruited from the area surrounding a university in the North Eastern United States.
Participants were eligible if they were monolingual English learners (no more than 25% exposure to a language besides English), and had no hearing or vision problems or other developmental delays.
An additional 15 participants were recruited, but excluded due to language exposure (n = 1), being in speech therapy (n = 9), technical difficulties (n = 2), or ending the experiment early (n = 3).
Participants completed the experiment with a research assistant in a quiet room.
Participants were told they were going to play a game where they would learn some new words.
A yellow box appeared around each icon, one at a time in randomized order, and participants were instructed to click on the icon with the box around it.
Participants were told they could choose to hear the word from anyone they wanted, and that they could choose the same person multiple times or pick different people.
Again, participants were told that they could choose to learn the new words from whoever they wanted, and to try their best to remember them.
First, during the Production Test, participants were asked to label the objects out loud.
Participants were encouraged to think about their answer and let the experimenter know when they were ready.
However, during the Familiarization and Learning phases, Passive participants were assigned to the order of choices made by an Active participant.
We used a strict approach to production accuracy: participants were considered to be accurate if they produced the target word (see Sinkeviciute et al., 2019).
Participants were considered to be accurate if they clicked on the target object.
However, participants were accurate on 13% of the productions they attempted.
In contrast to production, the comprehension task revealed successful word learning, participants were significantly above chance at learning the six novel word-object pairs.

info.title: Running head: ACTIVE LEARNING, TALKER VARIABILITY, AND WORD LEARNING Effects of active learning and talker variability on preschoolers' novel word learning

text.text: Words sound different every time they are said, both by the same person and across people.
This variability has been found to have mixed effects on learning, sometimes benefitting learning and other times making it more challenging.
However, all prior studies investigating effects of talker variability have used passive exposure, presenting participants with predetermined orders or fixed types of variability.
Here, we used a novel active learning paradigm wherein 3-and 4-year old preschoolers could choose who to hear words from during word learning.

Then, we tested whether participants seek out variability during word learning, how these talker variability choices influence word learning and whether actively making these choices results in different outcomes than passively receiving them.
We find that preschoolers choose to hear words from multiple talkers, but that talker variability does not predict word learning.

Taken together, our results suggest that preschool aged children do seek out variability, but that word learning outcomes are most predictived by their relative vocabulary sizes and not talker variability choices.
These results inform theories on the roles of both talker variability and active learning in language learning.
A challenge for language learners is that words sound different every time they are said, within and between talkers (Bulgarelli et al., 2021).
text.formatted: A challenge for language learners is that words sound different every time they are said, within and between talkers <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bulgarelli et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: How this talker variability influences learning remains an open question.
Early research suggested that talker variability may be something to overcome, or ignore, through the process of invariance detection (e.g. Gogate & Hollich, 2010).
text.formatted: Early research suggested that talker variability may be something to overcome, or ignore, through the process of invariance detection (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Gogate & Hollich, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: However, more recent research suggests that learners attend to talker variability, and that it influences learning (Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2022 , 2023).

text.text: Here, we capitalize on recent active learning paradigms, which allow participants to make choices about what and/or how to learn (e.g. Zettersten & Saffran, 2021), to ask whether preschoolers seek out talker variability during word learning, and how these choices influence learning.

text.text: Talker variability is a common feature of children's language experiences.

Recent studies using daylong recordings find that infants hear common words from 5 different talkers on average, and that hearing more talkers increases acoustic variability (Bulgarelli et al., 2021).

text.text: In turn, this variability influences word learning. Bulgarelli and Bergelson (2024) found that including measurements of acoustic variability (such as variability in mean pitch and duration) predicted more variance in when infants first produced words relative to just including frequency of each word.
text.formatted: In turn, this variability influences word learning. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bulgarelli and Bergelson (2024)</ref> found that including measurements of acoustic variability (such as variability in mean pitch and duration) predicted more variance in when infants first produced words relative to just including frequency of each word.

text.text: Similarly, words heard by more people were produced more frequently in at home recordings (Goldenberg et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Similarly, words heard by more people were produced more frequently in at home recordings <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Goldenberg et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Taking another approach, Zhao et al. (2025) measured the number of talkers of different ages 2-year-olds interacted with using a questionnaire, and found that interacting with a larger number of mature speakers (operationalized as 5th grade or older, or adults) predicted larger vocabulary sizes.

text.text: Thus, infants' experiences with talker variability shape their own word learning and use.

Besides more recent research establishing that variability is present in children's realworld input, the majority of research on talker variability has manipulated it in lab settings to study how it influences word recognition and learning.
In these in-lab studies, the effects of talker variability are mixed.
In some cases, talker variability benefits learning.

For example, research using the Switch task (Stager & Werker, 1997) finds that 14-month-olds are only able to learn novel minimal pairs when they are taught from multiple talkers (Hoehle et al., 2020; Rost & McMurray, 2009).

text.text: Similarly, talker variability helps 8-month-olds generalize newly learned words to novel talkers (Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2022).
text.formatted: Similarly, talker variability helps 8-month-olds generalize newly learned words to novel talkers <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Further, Richtsmeier et al. (2009) found that talker variability supported preschoolers' learning to produce novel words.
text.formatted: Further, <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Richtsmeier et al. (2009)</ref> found that talker variability supported preschoolers' learning to produce novel words.

text.text: In contrast, talker variability does not always support learning.

For example, while talker variability benefits learning novel minimal pairs, it inhibits learning of distinct sounding words that can be learned in the absence of variability (Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2023).
text.formatted: For example, while talker variability benefits learning novel minimal pairs, it inhibits learning of distinct sounding words that can be learned in the absence of variability <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, while talker variability helped 8-month-olds generalize words to new talkers, it resulted in overextending what "counts" as an instance of a newly-learned word (Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2022).
text.formatted: Similarly, while talker variability helped 8-month-olds generalize words to new talkers, it resulted in overextending what "counts" as an instance of a newly-learned word <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In other contexts, talker variability is found to be unrelated to learning.
Specifically, Sinkeviciute et al. (2019) found that talker variability did not affect novel word learning for 7-10 year olds, when tested in production or comprehension.

text.text: Further, cross-situational word learning is not aided or hindered by the presence of talker variability (Crespo et al., 2024; Crespo & Kaushanskaya, 2021), when tested in production or comprehension (Contino et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Further, cross-situational word learning is not aided or hindered by the presence of talker variability <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Crespo et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Crespo & Kaushanskaya, 2021)</ref>, when tested in production or comprehension <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Contino et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, effects of talker variability on word learning range from making the task more difficult (e.g. Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2023), to not affecting learning (e.g. Crespo et al., 2024) to benefiting learning (Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2024; e.g. Richtsmeier et al., 2009).

text.text: Recently, Tippenhauer (2026) proposed a unified account of the role of variability in word learning, proposing that there may be a desirable level of variability that interacts with both the learner, and the stage of learning (i.e. mapping words to meaning, retention, generalization).

Specifically, variability may be particularly beneficial when it highlights invariant dimensions of the stimuli, allowing the learner to attend to the features of a word that remain consistent across irrelevant variation (see also Rost & McMurray, 2009) and for generalization to novel instances (Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2022; Houston & Jusczyk, 2000; Quam & Creel, 2021; see also Raviv et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Specifically, variability may be particularly beneficial when it highlights invariant dimensions of the stimuli, allowing the learner to attend to the features of a word that remain consistent across irrelevant variation (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Rost & McMurray, 2009)</ref> and for generalization to novel instances <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Houston & Jusczyk, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Quam & Creel, 2021</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Raviv et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: When the balance of relevant and irrelevant variability is not "desirable", learners may not be able to home in on what features to attend to, which may interfere with learning.
However, Tippenhauer (2026) predicts that learners' age and cognitive skills can shift whether variability is helpful or challenging for learners (see also Goldenberg & Sandhofer, 2013).
text.formatted: However, <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Tippenhauer (2026)</ref> predicts that learners' age and cognitive skills can shift whether variability is helpful or challenging for learners (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Goldenberg & Sandhofer, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: For example, they suggest that learners' domain-specific knowledge about how words map to the world, which is refined as their vocabulary grows, can moderate the effect of variability.
That is, learners with more breadth and/or depth of vocabulary (Hadley & Dickinson, 2020) may be better able to capitalize on variability during word learning.
text.formatted: That is, learners with more breadth and/or depth of vocabulary <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Hadley & Dickinson, 2020</ref>) may be better able to capitalize on variability during word learning.

text.text: Another aspect of word learning that is not discussed in the Tippenhauer (2026) framework is how word learning is evaluated.
Across development, word knowledge is evaluated in different ways, spanning from receptive to expressive methods, and each of these outcome measures could reveal different effects of variability.

Specifically, comprehension seems to precede and/or outperform production, across development (Gershkoff-Stowe & Hahn, 2013). Hu et al. (2025) suggest that this asymmetry may be related to the more difficult task of producing a ACTIVE LEARNING, TALKER VARIABILITY, AND WORD LEARNING word -which requires selecting a particular sequence of sounds to produce -relative to choosing the correct reference out of a series of options -which significantly constrains the number of choices.

text.text: A separate line of research argues that children are active, motivated learners who structure their own learning through attention, active interventions on their environment (Raz & Saxe, 2020), and goal directed search for information (Saylor & Ganea, 2018).

text.text: For example, young children explore unfamiliar objects to reduce uncertainty (Sim & Xu, 2017), elicit labels from adults (e.g. Lucca & Wilbourn, 2018) and actively seek out information they want to attend to (such as overheard speech; Foushee et al. (2021)).

text.text: Some of this prior research also finds that active information seeking can lead to a "boost" in learning, such that children retain information better that they selected to learn themselves (De Simone & Ruggeri, 2022), though these effects in early childhood are mixed (see Ackermann et al., 2020; Bazhydai et al., 2026).

text.text: More recent research has shifted to other types of sampling behaviors.
For example, Sia et al. (2025) allowed children to choose how to learn, asking whether they wanted to actively sample information or receive it passively.

text.text: In the current manuscript, we extend this active learning approach to asking whether preschoolers choose to hear words from multiple talkers during the process of word learning.
Specifically, one proposal is that active learning is beneficial because learners will seek out information that reduces uncertainty (Kidd & Hayden, 2015).
text.formatted: Specifically, one proposal is that active learning is beneficial because learners will seek out information that reduces uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Kidd & Hayden, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: If talker variability is desirable for learning novel word-object mappings because it highlights how words remain consistent across varying speakers, then participants may seek it out to support word learning, and its effects should be consistent for participants who choose it themselves and for those who receive it.

However, an alternative is that active learning is driven by individual interest, and benefits of active learning may be due to higher task engagement for active relative to passive learners (Markant et al., 2014).

text.text: In this case, participants may make talker variability choices that are more interesting for them (see also Tippenhauer, 2026), but their effects may not generalize to participants who passively receive them.

text.text: Here, we designed a novel word learning paradigm to investigate whether preschoolers choose to hear talker variability during word learning, and how these choices influence learning.

Participants in the Active condition were given the choice of who to hear novel words from; they could choose to hear each word 8 times from 1 talker, 1 time from 8 talkers, or some combination in between.
Participants in the Passive condition received the exposure selected by a yoked Active participant, thus equating learning experiences across conditions but manipulating active information seeking.
Participants were then tested on their learning of the novel words, both in production and comprehension.

We tested 3-and 4-year-olds, an age at which prior research finds that talker variability supports learning to produce novel words (Richtsmeier et al., 2009) ACTIVE LEARNING, TALKER VARIABILITY, AND WORD LEARNING and at which children actively seek information to reduce ambiguity about word-object mappings (Zettersten et al., under review; Zettersten & Saffran, 2021).
text.formatted: We tested 3-and 4-year-olds, an age at which prior research finds that talker variability supports learning to produce novel words <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Richtsmeier et al., 2009)</ref> ACTIVE LEARNING, TALKER VARIABILITY, AND WORD LEARNING and at which children actively seek information to reduce ambiguity about word-object mappings <ref type="bibr">(Zettersten et al., under review;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Zettersten & Saffran, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Using this novel paradigm, we ask three questions: RQ1: Do preschoolers seek out talker variability during word learning?
RQ2: Does talker variability influence word learning, measured as both production and comprehension?
RQ3: Does actively choosing variability benefit learning differently than passively receiving it?
While talker variability can benefit learning, both in the lab and in the real world, we do not know whether preschoolers actively seek this out.
RQ1 will allow insight into participants' choices during word learning.
RQ2 will then test whether participants' talker variability choices support their learning.

Prior research suggests that talker variability may be particularly beneficial for preschoolers learning to produce novel words (Richtsmeier et al., 2009; though see Contino et al., 2026), and thus participants who hear more variability may exhibit better production accuracy.
text.formatted: Prior research suggests that talker variability may be particularly beneficial for preschoolers learning to produce novel words <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Richtsmeier et al., 2009</ref>; though see <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Contino et al., 2026)</ref>, and thus participants who hear more variability may exhibit better production accuracy.

text.text: In contrast, the effects of talker variability on forming word-object mappings is less consistent when words are distinct (i.e. not minimal pairs) (Bulgarelli & Bergelson, 2023), and during early childhood and preschool years (Crespo et al., 2024; Crespo & Kaushanskaya, 2021; Sinkeviciute et al., 2019), and thus talker variability may not influence comprehension accuracy.

text.text: RQ3 will test whether effects of talker variability differ for participants in the Active condition relative to those in the Passive condition.

If active information seeking is beneficial more generally, or if participants are choosing talker variability that is optimally useful or interesting for them, then we expect a benefit for learning in the Active condition.

However, it is also possible that participants choose variability that is sufficiently useful for learning, and that participants in the passive condition will be able to learn from it just as well, in which case we may not find an effect of condition (such that active and passive participants may exhibit similar learning).

An interaction between talker variability and condition would suggest that talker variability differentially influences learning for participants who actively choose it relative to those who passively receive it.

Participants were recruited from the area surrounding a university in the North Eastern United States.
Participants were eligible if they were monolingual English learners (no more than 25% exposure to a language besides English), and had no hearing or vision problems or other developmental delays.
An additional 15 participants were recruited, but excluded due to language exposure (n = 1), being in speech therapy (n = 9), technical difficulties (n = 2), or ending the experiment early (n = 3).
This study was approved by the University at Buffalo IRB and we obtained informed consent from participants' parents before data collection.
Stimuli consisted of 2 familiar objects and their corresponding labels (ball, apple), and 6 novel objects and their corresponding novel word labels.
The novel objects were chosen from the Novel Object and Unusual Name (NOUN) Database (Horst & Hout, 2016), and the novel words were bysillabic and followed conventional rules of English.

text.text: Participants were told they were going to play a game where they would learn some new words.
They sat at a table facing a 2-in-1 touchscreen laptop ACTIVE LEARNING, TALKER VARIABILITY, AND WORD LEARNING set up to function like a tablet.

The experiment consisted of five phases (Introduction, Familiarization, Learning, Production Test, and Comprehension Test, see Figure 1), followed by the NIH Toolbox vocabulary test (Gershon et al., 2014) to measure their receptive vocabulary.

text.text: We first describe the procedure for the Active condition, and then highlight differences in the Passive condition.
The Introduction phase served to expose participants to all the talkers in the study, and to teach them the task.
They were told they are going to meet all the people who they could learn new words from.
They saw a cartoon image of a waving hand in the middle of the screen, surrounded by eight different colored icons in a circle, representing eight different talkers (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: They saw a cartoon image of a waving hand in the middle of the screen, surrounded by eight different colored icons in a circle, representing eight different talkers (see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: A yellow box appeared around each icon, one at a time in randomized order, and participants were instructed to click on the icon with the box around it.
After clicking, all other icons disappeared and the talker said "Hi, it's nice to meet you."
Participants repeated this until they heard all eight talkers.
During the Familiarization phase, participants saw an image of a familiar item (apple, ball) in the middle of the screen, surrounded by the same eight talker icons.
They were told they were going to practice playing the game with some words they already know.
Participants were told they could choose to hear the word from anyone they wanted, and that they could choose the same person multiple times or pick different people.
Each object remained on the screen until they made 8 choices.
When participants clicked on one of the talker icons, all other icons disappeared and participants heard the talker label the image (e.g. apple).
This process was repeated for the other familiar word (e.g., ball, order counterbalanced across participants).
The Learning phase was similar to the Familiarization phase, but with the six novel objects and labels.
The order of novel object presentation was randomized.
Again, participants were told that they could choose to learn the new words from whoever they wanted, and to try their best to remember them.
When they clicked on a talker icon, all other icons disappeared and they heard the talker they chose produce the label.
Participants heard each word 8 times, before moving on to another novel word-object pair.
This process was repeated for all 6 novel word-object pairs.
Participants' learning was then measured with two different test phases.
First, during the Production Test, participants were asked to label the objects out loud.
On each trial, participants saw an object in the center of the screen, and were asked to label it.

text.text: We tested whether preschoolers chose to hear words from multiple talkers during word learning, and whether those choices had an effect on learning.

We found that participants do choose to hear words from multiple talkers, hearing 6 different talkers on average (out of a possible 8), but that actively or passively received talker variability did not influence word learning.
We also found that individual differences in vocabulary size predicted learning in the passive but not active condition.

Taken together, this study provides novel insights into participants' word learning choices and their effects on learning, highlighting that while hearing more talkers may be the modal choice for preschoolers, it may not directly influence learning outcomes.
Research suggests that talker variability can benefit aspects of novel word learning.
Here, we asked whether preschoolers therefore seek out variability when learning novel words.
After being introduced to all talkers, such that participants would not choose to hear all of them out of curiosity, preschoolers chose to hear novel words from 6 talkers on average.
Participants chose approximately the same number of talkers for the novel and familiar words, suggesting that preschoolers may value hearing multiple talkers, or generally find it more interesting.
Nonetheless, individual participants varied in the extent to which they chose more or less variability, with a few participants (n= 2) choosing to hear just 1-2 talkers for each word.

Talker variability choices also varied by participant factors, such that participants with relatively larger age-normed vocabulary sizes selected more variability overall. Tippenhauer (2026) suggests that children must possess a specific level of knowledge about how words map to meaning to determine which features of variability could be relevant for word learning, and this may be evidenced by measuring the depth of their vocabulary.

text.text: The pattern of talker variability choices evidenced here might suggest that preschoolers with relatively larger vocabulary sizes may have identified that talker variability could support word learning, and selected more talkers accordingly.

At the same time, prior research suggests that talker variability may make the task more interesting (Crespo & Kaushanskaya, 2021; Tippenhauer, 2026), and thus participants with larger vocabularies here may have found the task less challenging and therefore sought out a more interesting experience.

text.text: While not directly measured here, participants' talker variability choices could also be related to their curiosity.

text.text: We tested two components of novel word learning: production and comprehension.
Despite participants readily producing the familiar words when asked, the rate of production attempts for novel words, and production accuracy more generally, was quite low.
For this reason, we were not able to model production accuracy statistically.

Despite some research finding that preschool aged children produce novel words during experimental tasks (Richtsmeier et al., 2009; see Contino et al., 2026 for older children), other studies also report low production accuracy at this age (Storkel & Lee, 2011), or report needing to exclude production tests overall due to toddlers rarely producing words (Gershkoff-Stowe & Hahn, 2013).

text.text: In the remainder of the discussion, we therefore focus on interpreting the patterns of results for the comprehension task.
Our paradigm allowed us to test whether talker variability and the ability to actively make choices about how to learn resulted in different patterns of learning.
We did not find overall ACTIVE LEARNING, TALKER VARIABILITY, AND WORD LEARNING effects of talker variability: accuracy on the comprehension task was not related to talker variability.
In some ways, this suggests that talker variability selected by participants may have been sufficient for learning.

In other ways, it could suggest that talker variability may be unrelated to learning for this task and age group, replicating and extending prior research using cross-situational statistical learning and word learning tasks (e.g. Crespo et al., 2024; Sinkeviciute et al., 2019) which finds that in early childhood, talker variability does not influence word-object mappings when the words are distinct from each other.

text.text: While talker variability did not predict learning, learning condition (Active vs.
Passive) did.
Specifically, we found that active learning interacted with age-normed receptive vocabulary size.

Here, participants in the Active condition exhibited similar comprehension accuracy regardless of vocabulary size, suggesting that preschoolers in the active condition may have made choices that optimized their interest and/or learning.
In contrast, participants in the Passive condition exhibited better learning if they had relatively larger vocabulary sizes.

The finding that participants with larger vocabulary sizes perform better on word learning tasks is consistent with previous research documenting a positive relationship between children's receptive knowledge and novel word learning (Gray, 2004; Hadley et al., 2021).

text.text: Here we extend this finding to show that preschoolers with larger vocabulary sizes are also better able to capitalize on talker variability chosen for them during word learning.
This is consistent with the proposal made by Tippenhauer (2026) that learners with greater depth and breadth of vocabulary may be better able to navigate relevant and irrelevant variability.
We recently conducted a similar study with adults (masked for review).
Instead of learning novel words paired with novel objects, adults were taught Lithuanian translations for common nouns (e.g. house, tree; Sinkeviciute et al. (2019)).

text.text: Similar to preschoolers, adult participants chose to hear novel words from 5 talkers on average.

However, for adults hearing more variability for individual words supported learning to produce and recognize these words, and participants in the passive condition outperformed those in the active condition on comprehension.
These findings suggest that, despite making relatively similar talker variability choices, the effects of talker variability and active learning may change over the course of development.

Previous research comparing adults and children in the same task is rare, but one study similarly found that while adults and preschoolers similarly sampled words to reduce ambiguity, these sampling strategies were only related to learning for adult and not preschoolaged participants (Zettersten & Saffran, 2021).

text.text: Taken together, we find that while preschoolers choose to hear talker variability during word learning, their talker variability choices are not related to learning outcomes.

We also found interactions between information seeking and age-normed vocabulary sizes, such that for participants in the yoked-passive condition, receptive vocabulary sizes were related to how well they were able to learn from someone elses's choices -participants with relatively larger vocabularies exhibited better word learning.

This study furthers our understanding of the types of choices children make during word learning, and highlights that active information seeking interacts with participant and task factors to support learning.
